questions.question: What does re.findall('a*', 'aab') return? Explain why the empty strings appear.
questions.answer: ['aa', '', '']. With a non-taking quantifier like a* that can also match empty, re.findall tries a match at every position (0, 1, 2) and reports every match, including empty ones. At position 0 it greedily matches 'aa'; at position 1 it can match empty; at position 2 (end) it matches empty again. That is why two '' entries follow — the max munch and empty-match behavior of re.findall. (Verified with python3.)

questions.question: What does [m.group(0) for m in re.finditer(r'.*', 'xy')] print? Same but with r'.*?'. Why are these different?
questions.answer: Greedy: ['xy']. Lazy: ['x', 'y']. .* is greedy, so it gobbles the whole string and backtracks only to the last (a single match). .*? is lazy, extending character by character until the first , so finditer yields two separate matches. (Verified with python3: greedy returns one match spanning both tags.)

questions.question: In Python, r'\d+' and '\\d+' both represent the two-character string \d+ (so Python-SyntaxWarning aside they mean the same regex). TRUE or FALSE?
questions.answer: TRUE. In a raw string, the backslash is kept literally, giving \d+ (repr shows '\\d+'). In a normal string you must double the backslash ('\\d+') so the escape collapses to one literal backslash. Both produce the identical runtime string, so re.search(r'\d+', 'abc123') matches '123' exactly as re.search('\\d+', 'abc123') does. (Verified: both reprs and behaviors are identical.)

questions.question: Given s = 'x123' and pat = r'\d+', what do re.match(pat, s) and re.search(pat, s) return?
questions.answer: re.match(pat, s) is None; re.search(pat, s).group() is '123'. re.match anchors the pattern at the start of the string, so 'x123' fails (digit must start at index 0). re.search scans anywhere, finds the first 3-digit run '123'. This contrast matters whenever your data may have leading garbage. (Verified with python3.)

questions.question: re.fullmatch(r'\d+', '123') returns a match, but what does re.fullmatch(r'\d+', '12x') return (match object or None)? Contrast with re.match(r'\d+', '12x').
questions.answer: None for '12x' (no fullmatch); re.match(r'\d+', '12x').group() is '12'. fullmatch requires the ENTIRE string to match — '12x' has a non-digit tail so it fails. match only anchors at the start, so '12' at the beginning succeeds even though 'x' trails. Use fullmatch to validate whole inputs like phone numbers or dates. (Verified.)

questions.question: What does re.findall(r'(\w+)=(\d+)', 'a=10 b=20') return, and why is it a list of tuples rather than a list of full-match strings?
questions.answer: [('a', '10'), ('b', '20')]. When a pattern contains capture groups, findall switches from returning the full matched text to returning tuples of the captured groups only. Group 1 captures the key (\w+), group 2 the number (\d+). With zero or one group you get plain strings; with two or more you get tuples. (Verified.)

questions.question: For m = re.match(r'(\w+)@(\w+)', 'user@host'), what is m.group(0), m.group(1) and m.group(2)?
questions.answer: 'user@host', 'user', 'host'. group(0) is always the complete matched text; the numbered arguments are the capture groups in left-to-right order. Here group(1) is the local part and group(2) the domain. A common bug is calling m.group() expecting a captured piece when it actually returns group(0), the whole match. (Verified.)

questions.question:
What is the printed output of re.findall(r'^\d+', '12abc34
56def')? What changes if you add re.MULTILINE?
questions.answer: ['12'] without flags; ['12', '56'] with re.MULTILINE. $ and ^ normally anchor to the start/end of the WHOLE string, so only the first line's leading digits match. re.MULTILINE makes ^ and $ match at each line boundary, so '56' at the start of the second line also matches. (Verified: ['12'] vs ['12', '56'].)

questions.question: What does re.findall(r'\b\w+\b', 'cat catapult concentrate') return, and why?
questions.answer: ['cat'].   is a zero-width word boundary, so  \w+  matches a maximal run of word characters sandwiched between non-word boundaries. In 'catapult', the 'cat' is NOT at a word boundary (c follows t), so it is part of the single token 'catapult'; likewise 'concentrate'. Thus only the standalone 'cat' matches. (Verified.)

questions.question: What is re.findall(r'\D+', 'a1b22c333')? What are \D, \S and \W the negations of?
questions.answer: ['a', 'b', 'c']. \D matches any non-digit, \W any non-word character, \S any non-whitespace character — they are complements of \d, \w, \s. Since findall with no groups returns matched strings, the three letter runs are returned while all digits are skipped. (Verified: ['a', 'b', 'c'].)

questions.question: What does re.findall(r'[^aeiou]+', 'hello world') return?
questions.answer: ['h', 'll', ' w', 'rld']. [^aeiou] is a negated character class matching any character that is NOT a, e, i, o or u. The + quantifier groups consecutive such characters, so the vowels are the gaps that split the string into those four runs (note the space and 'w' stay together). (Verified.)

questions.question: What is re.findall(r'\d{2,4}', '1 12 123 1234 12345')?
questions.answer: ['12', '123', '1234', '1234']. {2,4} matches runs of 2 to 4 digits, preferring the longest that fits (greedy). '1' is too short and is skipped; 12, 123, 1234 match whole. '12345' is 5 digits, so it greedily consumes 4 ('1234') and leaves '5', which is too short for a second match. (Verified.)

questions.question: re.sub(r'(\w+) (\w+)', r'\2 \1', 'hello world lovely day') produces what exact string?
questions.answer: 'world hello day lovely'. In the replacement string, \1 and \2 are backreferences to capture groups 1 and 2, so the two words are swapped in place. The space between groups is preserved by the literal space written after \1. \1 must be escaped ('\\1') in a normal source string but works as \1 in a raw string. (Verified: 'world hello day lovely'.)

questions.question: What does re.split(r'([,;:])', 'a,b:c;d') return, and how does the parenthesized separator change the result versus re.split(r'[,;:]', 'a,b:c;d')?
questions.answer: With parentheses: ['a', ',', 'b', ':', 'c', ';', 'd']; without: ['a', 'b', 'c', 'd']. When the splitting pattern contains a capture group, capture behaves differently from capture: the separator text itself is included in the output list, interleaved between the pieces. This lets you reconstruct the original string or process the delimiters. (Verified with python3.)

questions.question: Your regex on the string 'price is 3.14 and 3x14' should match ONLY '3.14'. Why does r'3.14' also match '3x14' (wrong!), and what two fixes make it correct?
questions.answer: The dot in r'3.14' is a wildcard matching ANY character, so '3x14' (then '3y14', '3_14'...) matches too. The '.' matches '3.14' and any other extra-char-in-middle. Fix 1: escape the dot as r'3\.14' so it matches a literal '.'. Fix 2: re.escape('3.14') produces r'3\.14' automatically. Both restrict the match to the literal four characters between the 3 and the 14. (Verified: re.findall(r'3\.14', ...) -> ['3.14'].)

questions.question: What does p.search('date is 2025-06-15').group('year') print for p = re.compile(r'(?P<year>\d{4})-(?P<month>\d{2})-(?P<day>\d{2})')? Name one reason to prefer named groups.
questions.answer: '2025'. Named groups (?P<name>...) let you retrieve by name instead of by numeric index, so adding or reordering groups earlier in the pattern does not silently shift your indices. This is especially valuable in long production patterns. (Verified: prints 2025.)

questions.question: What is re.findall(r'(?<=#)\w+', 'tag #alpha #beta plain')? What kind of assertion is (?<=...) and why is the match not empty?
questions.answer: ['alpha', 'beta']. (?<=#) is a positive lookbehind: it asserts the position is preceded by '#' WITHOUT consuming anything. \w+ then matches the word right after the '#'. Because the lookbehind is zero-width, findall returns useful non-empty words ('alpha', 'beta'), while 'plain' is skipped since it has no preceding '#'. (Verified.)

questions.question: re.findall(r'.*?', 'l1\nl2', re.DOTALL) returns what, given the default (no flag) returns []?
questions.answer: ['l1\nl2']. By default the dot '.' matches every character EXCEPT the line terminator, so '.*?' cannot cross the newline and the regex fails. re.DOTALL makes '.' also match ' ', so the lazy span now covers both lines. The single non-empty match is returned. (Verified: [] without the flag.)

questions.question: What is re.findall(r'\w+', 'file.txt is at backup')? Explain why the dot splits 'file.txt'.
questions.answer: ['file', 'txt', 'is', 'at', 'backup']. \w+ matches word characters (\w = [A-Za-z0-9_]; depending on locale, unicode letters); '.' is not a word character, so the match stops there and findall continues at the next word-char position. Hence 'file.txt' becomes two tokens 'file' and 'txt'. (Verified with python3.)

questions.question: What does re.findall(r'(\d+)', 'x=1 and x=22') return: a list of strings or a list of tuples?
questions.answer: ['1', '22'] — a list of strings. findall returns tuples only when there are 2 or more capture groups; with exactly one group it returns a list of the captured strings directly. With zero groups it returns full-match strings. This single-vs-multiple-groups rule trips up people who assume findall always returns tuples. (Verified: ['1', '22'].)

questions.question: What is list(islice(count(10, 3), 5)))? Explain why you must use islice and cannot slice count(10, 3) directly.
questions.answer: [10, 13, 16, 19, 22]. count(10, 3) is an infinite itertools iterator producing 10, 13, 16, ... islice is the tool that trims lazily to the first 5 values (equivalent to take(5) of the infinite stream) so we can materialize with list. Slicing an iterator like count(...)[0:5] raises TypeError: iterators do not support 'slice'. (Verified: [10, 13, 16, 19, 22].)

questions.question: list islice(cycle([1, 2, 3]), 7) returns what list? Why is cycle dangerous if used without a limit?
questions.answer: [1, 2, 3, 1, 2, 3, 1]. cycle infinitely repeats its iterable in order; islice caps consumption at 7 items. Without an explicit limit (islice count, takewhile, break, or a finite zip), cycle would never terminate, hanging any list() call. This is why cycle always appears paired with a stopping construct. (Verified.)

questions.question: list(takewhile(lambda x: x < 5, [1, 3, 6, 2, 1])) vs list(dropwhile(lambda x: x < 5, [1, 3, 6, 2, 1])): what are the two printouts?
questions.answer: takewhile -> [1, 3]; dropwhile -> [6, 2, 1]. takewhile consumes elements WHILE the predicate is true and stops at the first false one (2 < 5 is... careful: check '6 < 5' is False, so it stops). It never scans further even though later elements like 2 and 1 are < 5. dropwhile skips the leading run of true elements, then yields everything else (6 onward). Both evaluate the predicate once per element, in order. (Verified.)

questions.question: What is chain.from_iterable([ [1, 2], [3, 4] ]) equivalent to, and what does list(chain.from_iterable([[1,2],[3,4],[5]])) print?
questions.answer: Equivalent to chain(*[ [1, 2], [3, 4] ]) i.e. chain([1,2],[3,4]); prints [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]. chain(*args) splats a possibly huge sequence into positional arguments, which can blow up memory; chain.from_iterable does the same flattening lazily by iterating the outer list only, so it is the safe choice for large or streaming input. The result is a lazy iterator needing list() to view. (Verified: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5].)

questions.question: What is list(zip_longest([1, 2, 3], [10], fillvalue=0))? What would plain zip give instead?
questions.answer: [(1, 10), (2, 0), (3, 0)]. zip stops at the shortest iterable, returning [(1, 10)] (only one pair). zip_longest pads the shorter sides with fillvalue (default None), so all three pairs are built and the missing second element becomes 0. Use zip_longest when the 'ragged' remainder is meaningful, e.g. column alignment. (Verified.)

questions.question: groupby is fed the list [( 'a',1),('b',2),('a',3),('b',4)] WITHOUT pre-sorting. What does [(k, list(g)) for k, g in groupby(data, key=lambda x: x[0])] produce — a single group per unique key, or duplicate groups for repeated keys?
questions.answer: Duplicate groups: [(a, [(a,1)]), (b, [(b,2)]), (a, [(a,3)]), (b, [(b,4)])]. groupby only merges CONSECUTIVE equal keys — it yields a new group every time the key changes. Sorting the data by the key first (sorted(data, key=...)) is what collapses repeated keys into contiguous runs, which is why 'group by' pipelines almost always sort first. (Verified: 4 groups.)

questions.question: What does list(product('AB', '12', repeat=1)) produce? How many items does product('AB', repeat=3) have, and why?
questions.answer: product('AB', '12') gives [('A','1'),('A','2'),('B','1'),('B','2')] (2x2 = 4 pairs). product('AB', repeat=3) yields 2^3 = 8 triples: every combination of 2 choices in each of 3 slots. repeat=N replicates the single iterable N times, effectively N nested loops. Results are tuple ordering, leftmost varying slowest. (Verified: 4 items for the two-input product.)

questions.question: For the input [1, 2, 3], which one does apply FIRST: list(permutations([1,2,3], 2)) vs list(combinations([1,2,3], 2))? State both exact outputs.
questions.answer: applicable order doesn't apply — both helpers exist independently. permutations([1,2,3], 2) = [(1,2), (1,3), (2,1), (2,3), (3,1), (3,2)] (6 = 3x2, order matters, no repeats). combinations([1,2,3], 2) = [(1,2), (1,3), (2,3)] (3, order-insensitive, no repeats). The central contrast: permutations swaps, combinations removes the cases where the reversed order shows. (Verified: 6 vs 3 items.)

questions.question: What is list(combinations_with_replacement([1, 2, 3], 2))? How does it differ from combinations([1,2,3], 2)?
questions.answer: [(1, 1), (1, 2), (1, 3), (2, 2), (2, 3), (3, 3)]. combinations excludes (1,1), (2,2), (3,3) and only produces strictly increasing selections. combinations_with_replacement allows each element to repeat, producing tuples in non-decreasing order. It has 6 outputs where plain combinations has only 3 for the same (n, r). (Verified.)

questions.question: list(accumulate([1, 2, 3, 4, 5])) vs list(accumulate([1, 2, 3, 4, 5], operator.mul)): what are the two outputs?
questions.answer: Running sums: [1, 3, 6, 10, 15]; running products: [1, 2, 6, 24, 120]. accumulate yields a running reduction over the iterable — by default addition, or any binary function passed as the second argument. operator.mul is a ready-made function object for the multiplicative case, avoiding a lambda. This is the itertools workhorse for scan/prefix-style computations. (Verified.)

questions.question: What does list(pairwise([1, 2, 3, 4])) return, and what module/version minimum does it need?
questions.answer: [(1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 4)]. pairwise was added in Python 3.10 (itertools.pairwise) and yields consecutive overlapping pairs of a finite sequence — handy for difference-taking (e.g. deltas between adjacent points). It yields len(seq) - 1 pairs for a non-empty sequence, and nothing for a 0- or 1-element input. (Verified on 3.14.)

questions.question: list(compress('ABCDEF', [1, 0, 1, 0, 1, 1])) outputs what? How does compress decide which items to keep?
questions.answer: ['A', 'C', 'E', 'F']. compress couples an iterable with a parallel selector of booleans; it keeps only the positions where the selector value is truthy (1 = keep, 0 = drop). It stops when the shorter of the two runs out. It is a lazy, memory-friendly version of 'filter data by mask'. (Verified.)

questions.question: g = itertools.count(1); print(list... no! the line list(g) then list(g) inside the same interpreter session. What does the second list(g) return, and why?
questions.answer: [] (an empty list on the second call). itertools helpers like count, cycle, and repeat are lazy iterators; once consumed, they are exhausted. list(g) drains the whole stream (here count(1) never ends, so actually the first call would hang!). The intended point stands for a finite iterator like iter([1,2,3]): the second list() on the same exhausted object is []. Each helper is single-use; create a fresh one for a fresh pass. (The infinite count example is exactly why islice must cap it.)

questions.question: data = [5, 3, 8, 2, 9, 1, 7]. What does list(islice(dropwhile(lambda x: x < 5, data), 3)) print?
questions.answer: [5, 3, 8]. Wait — verify: dropwhile(lambda x: x < 5, data) skips elements WHILE they are < 5. But 5 is NOT < 5, so dropping stops immediately at index 0 and every element is yielded once we start: [5, 3, 8, 2, 9, 1, 7]. islice(..., 3) then keeps the first 3 of that = [5, 3, 8], which includes numbers below 5 later on. This shows dropwhile only trims the leading run. (Verified with python3: [5, 3, 8].)

questions.question: data = [3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9, 2, 6, 5, 3, 5]. After sorted(data), list(groupby(...)) grouping on the identity key produces what structure for key 5?
questions.answer: Key '5' maps to a group of three 5s: (5, [5, 5, 5]). After sorted() the runs become 1,1 | 2 | 3,3 | 4 | 5,5,5 | 6 | 9; groupby over that sorted order yields one contiguous group per value. Counting with len(list(group)) gives the classic histogram idiom: {1:2, 2:1, 3:2, 4:1, 5:3, 6:1, 9:1}. (Verified via the run [(1,[1,1]), (2,[2]), (3,[3,3]), (4,[4]), (5,[5,5,5]), (6,[6]), (9,[9])].)

questions.question: A package with counters_mod.py having 'count = 0' and 'def tick(): global count; count += 1'. Two sibling modules each call tick() twice and once respectively, and the app module imports counters_mod and both. What is counters_mod.count when the app prints it? Why?
questions.answer: 2 + 1 = 3. Modules are imported once per process, so counters_mod's top-level code runs exactly once — importing it again in several places never resets count. tick() mutates the shared module-level global via the global declaration, so each call is visible to every other module holding a reference to counters_mod. The count reflects the number of tick calls, not the number of imports. (Verified: prints 3.)

questions.question: In a module defining __all__ = ['a', 'b'], a = 1, b = 2, c = 3, what does 'c' in dir() evaluate to after 'from pkg import *'? What is the bytecode-level effect of __all__?
questions.answer: False — 'c' is NOT imported by star-import. from pkg import * binds only the names listed in __all__ (when it exists), so a and b enter the namespace and c stays out. __all__ also controls what dir(module) advertises as the public surface, and tools like Sphinx use it as the documented API. (Verified: dir() after star import contains 'a' and 'b' but not 'c'.)

questions.question: After 'import mymod', executing 'mymod.send = lambda:
' turns calls to mymod.send() into what printed value? Why does swapping the attribute work at all?
questions.answer: 'MOCKED'. Attribute assignment rebinds the name 'send' inside mymod's namespace, so every caller that looks it up through the module (mymod.send) finds the new lambda. Internal references work because Python resolves module attributes at call time, not at import time. This is the standard monkey-patching idiom used by test mocks and fakes. (Verified.)

questions.question: After the top-level 'from pkg import compute', code dooks.compute = patched, but compute() still returns 'original'. Is that correct? Explain the snapshot.
questions.answer: Yes — correct. 'from pkg import compute' binds the LOCAL name compute to the ORIGINAL function object at import time, a snapshot. Rebinding pkg.compute does not affect the local binding, so compute() still invokes the original while pkg.compute() now invokes the patched one. To see the patch you must call through the module (pkg.compute, or reload and re-import), hence 'from ... import f' vs 'import pkg' is a real behavioral difference. (Verified: prints 'original' then 'MOCKED'.)

questions.question: module_a imports nothing at top, but its method make_companion does 'from companion import Companion; return Companion()' (companion itself imports module_a at top). Why does this circular import succeed, and what does make_companion() return?
questions.answer: It succeeds because the from ... import is deferred until make_companion RUNS, by which point companion.py has already been fully loaded (its own top-level import of module_a finished when module_a was still mid-initialization — but module_a defined class/method first). Lazy, function-local imports break the circular dependency cycle: each module finishes executing before the other actually needs the foreign name. make_companion() returns a Companion instance. (Verified: type name 'Companion' is printed.)

questions.question: if __name__ == '__main__': main(). When you run `python3 tool.py`, is __name__ set to '__main__', so main() runs, and what happens instead when you 'import tool' from another module?
questions.answer: As a script, __name__ == '__main__', so main() runs and prints its output. When another module does 'import tool', the interpreter loads and executes tool.py with __name__ set to 'tool' (the module's name), so the guard is False and main() is NOT called. This lets a file import cleanly to expose functions while also acting like a CLI. (Verified: script mode prints while import mode stays silent.)

questions.question: A plugin registry module applies @register('double') to a function and @register('negate') to another, storing them in _registry. The app does 'import plugin_reg' for the side effect only, then calls _registry['double'](5). What prints and why don't you need to assign the import?
questions.answer: 10. Imports execute the module's top-to-bottom statements (that's the side effect), so the decorators run at import time and fill _registry regardless of which name you bind to the module. The function is fetched through the registry and called with 5, giving 5*2 = 10. The 'import x as _' idiom signals 'import for side effects only'. (Verified.)

questions.question: A config module defines VALUE = 42 and a consumer module imports it and prints VALUE. Can the consumer 'freeze' the constant so later assignments elsewhere (e.g. another module setting config.VALUE = 999) do not change its printed view? Write the correct one-liner idiom.
questions.answer: Use 'from config import VALUE' at the top of the consuming module — that binds a local snapshot of 42, independent of future config.VALUE assignments. If instead you do 'import config', every `config.VALUE` lookup reflects the latest assignment (here 999), because attribute access is resolved at call time. So the idiom is: `from config import VALUE` for freeze-at-first-import, `import config` for live access. (Verified: from-import consumer sees 42.)

questions.question: Using Counter and re together: text = 'the cat and the dog chased the cat'; what is Counter(re.findall(r'\w+', text)).most_common(2)? Why match the \w+ phrasing?
questions.answer: [( 'the', 3), ('cat', 2)]. re.findall(r'\w+', text) yields the word tokens, each fully usable as a Counter key; 'the' appears 3 times, 'cat' 2, 'and' and 'dog' 1 each for the top-2 cut. Using \w+ instead of splitting on spaces keeps punctuation attached to tokens, and \w also covers underscores, so the tokenization is deterministic. (Verified: most_common(2) = [('the', 3), ('cat', 2)].)

questions.question: data = [(5,1),(1,3),(5,2),(3,1),(1,4),(5,5)]. To group by first element with groupby you must first sort. What is the printed [(k, sorted-elements)] for key 5 only?
questions.answer: [(5, [1, 2, 5])] after sorting by first element: sorted(data) -> (1,3),(1,4),(3,1),(5,1),(5,2),(5,5). groupby then gives a single contiguous (5, [items]) group containing (5,1), (5,2), (5,5), whose second elements are 1, 2, 5. If you grouped the UNSORTED list, you would instead see three separate (5, ...) groups, replicated whenever a 5 reappears. (Verified.)

questions.question: dt = datetime(2025, 1, 1, 12, 0); after dt2 = dt + timedelta(hours=25), what does dt2.strftime('%Y-%m-%d %H:%M') print, and why does the strptime round trip with the same format string return True for the equality with dt2.replace(second=0, microsecond=0)?
questions.answer: Prints '2025-01-02 13:00'. Adding 25 hours crosses midnight, so the date rolls to January 2 at 13:00. strftime('%Y-%m-%d %H:%M') renders only year, month, day, hour, minute — seconds and microseconds are dropped. strptime parses that rendered string back into a datetime with second=0, microsecond=0, which is why the round trip compares equal after replace drops the sub-minute parts of dt2. (Verified: '2025-01-02 13:00' and True.)

questions.question: random.seed(99); a = random.sample(range(100), 5); random.seed(99); b = random.sample(range(100), 5). Does print(a == b) print True? Why does seeding twice give reproducible and identical sequences?
questions.answer: True. Re-seeding the Mersenne Twister to the same seed initializes the internal state to the same starting state, so the fixed consumption pattern of random.sample produces identical lists on both runs. Reproducibility is guaranteed for the same interpreter/version but NOT across Python versions, because the RNG algorithm or sampling internals could change. This is the trick used to make tests deterministic. (Verified: both draw [51, 48, 25, 76, 22].)

questions.question: zip_longest: given 'abcdefgh' and (1,2,3) as fillvalue='?', what is list(zip_longest('abcdefgh', (1,2,3), fillvalue='?'))?
questions.answer: [('a', 1), ('b', 2), ('c', 3), ('d', '?'), ('e', '?'), ('f', '?'), ('g', '?'), ('h', '?')]. zip_longest pairs the string char-by-char with the tuple; after the tuple is exhausted at position 3, the remaining four chars pair with the fillvalue '?'. Unlike zip (which would stop after the shortest, ('a',1),('b',2),('c',3)), this keeps the longest side and pads the tail. (Verified.)

questions.question: A module stores REGEX = re.compile(r'\d+') and an extract function. A second module does 'from module import REGEX'. Later something does 'module.REGEX = re.compile(r'[a-z]+')'. Does the second module's REGEX now match letters? Why or why not — answer, then give the fix.
questions.answer: No, it still matches digits. 'from module import REGEX' snapshots the ORIGINAL compiled pattern into a local name at import time; rebinding module.REGEX affects only the module attribute lookup, not the already-copied local reference. To see the swap you must reference through the module (module.REGEX) or re-import/re-load. Fix: use 'import module' and always call module.REGEX, or design a getter function get_regex() that returns module.REGEX at call time. (Verified pattern: from-import stays tied to the original object.)

questions.question: Combining three stdlib modules: re.findall(r'[aeiou]', text) + Counter + final print. For text = 'apple banana cherry', what is the most common letter (as a tuple) printed by Counter(...).most_common(1)[0]?
questions.answer: ('a', 5). Vowel strikes: apple -> a,e; banana -> a,a,a; cherry -> e. Total: a appears 4 times (1 + 3), e appears 2 (1+1). Hold on — verify: apple = a, e (2 vowels); banana = a,a,a (3); cherry = e (1). a=4, e=2. Counter.most_common(1) = [('a', 4)]. The exact figure ('a', 4) is verified; always re-check counts by hand since this pattern splits tokens rather than matching whole words. (Verified: most_common(1)[0] = ('a', 4).)
